title: They grant the decrees to permit or effect acts precede foreknowledge of the absolutely future determination (Adam, Paul)
source_text: XXV. Hoc posito concedunt decreta Dei circa actus humanos, vel permittendos, vel efficiendos, in Deo, juxta nostrum concipiendi modum, antecedere praescientiam determinationis voluntatis humanae, quae absolute futura sit. Deus enim verbi causa, ex eorum mente, decrevit permittere ut Adamus pomum vetitum appeteret, & ad actum istum cum eo concurrere, priusquam absolute praeviderit Adami voluntatem eo se determinaturam. Et prius decrevit Paulum gratia sua praevenire, & cum eo ad conversionis actum cooperari, quam absolute praeviderit fore ut Pauli voluntas ad hoc se determinaret.
pass_a_gloss: XXV. This being posited, they concede that the decrees of God concerning human acts, either to be permitted, or to be effected, precede in God, according to our mode of conceiving, the foreknowledge of the determination of the human will, which is to be absolutely future. For God for example, according to their mind, decreed to permit that Adam should desire the forbidden apple, and to concur with him to that act, before he absolutely foresaw that Adam's will would determine itself to it. And he decreed to prevent Paul with his grace, and to cooperate with him to the act of conversion, before he absolutely foresaw that Paul's will would determine itself to this.
pass_b_english: On this basis they grant that God's decrees about human acts, whether to permit them or to bring them about, come before his foreknowledge of the human will's absolutely future determination, according to our way of conceiving things in God.

On their view, for example, God decreed to permit Adam to desire the forbidden fruit, and to concur with him in that act, before he absolutely foresaw that Adam's will would determine itself to it. Likewise he decreed to anticipate Paul with his grace and to cooperate with him in the act of conversion before he absolutely foresaw that Paul's will would determine itself to it.
